tagline.text: A 1977 presidential retreat museum overlooking Paoay Lake

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Suba, Paoay, Ilocos Norte, on the hill west of Paoay Lake

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300~1,000 (per person, based on a half-day trip from Laoag including admission, transport and meals)

children.text: Malacañang of the North is a two-story mansion built on the shore of Paoay Lake in 1977 by the Philippine Tourism Authority as a gift for President Marcos's 60th birthday, and it is now a museum run by the Ilocos Norte provincial government. Its seven rooms are set up around the president's main policy themes, and a balcony gives a full view of the lake.

Malacañang of the North (Malacañang ti Amianan in Ilocano) is a presidential museum in Barangay Suba, Paoay, Ilocos Norte. According to Wikipedia, the Philippine Tourism Authority (now TIEZA) built it in 1977 for President Ferdinand Marcos's 60th birthday, and it stands as a two-story bahay na bato (stone-house style) mansion on a site of about 5 hectares overlooking Paoay Lake. As its nickname "Malacañang of the North," borrowed from the name of the presidential residence in Manila, suggests, it was the official residence the president's family used when staying in Ilocos, and it comes up whenever the recent history of Batac and Paoay is discussed.

The building was made with local materials. Floors, wall panels and doors are Philippine hardwood, and the sliding windows are fitted with capiz shells. The ground floor has a large reception hall that can hold about 100 people, a wide wooden staircase rising on the left, and a dining hall; the second floor has a spacious bedroom, a library and an office where officials were received. There are seven rooms in all, and the number seven is said to have been lucky for Marcos. From the balcony you see a large garden and, beyond it, the lake, and the lake view is one of the biggest attractions.

The current exhibits were arranged after 2010. That year the Benigno Aquino III government handed use of the building to the Ilocos Norte provincial government, and Imee Marcos, the president's daughter and then governor, had it refurbished as a tourist attraction. Eric Zerrudo of the University of Santo Tomas's Center for Conservation of Cultural Property and Environment in the Tropics was commissioned to curate the exhibits, setting seven themes, with the rooms devoted to Study, Agriculture, Diplomacy, overseas workers (OFWs), Culture, Nation Building and Family, each explaining one of the Marcos government's programs. It is also recorded that in 2014 the Sandiganbayan anti-graft court stripped the Marcos family of rights to the property and voided the 1978 agreement between Marcos and the Tourism Authority, on the grounds that national park land is inalienable public domain.

What travelers should know is that this is not a purely cultural-heritage museum but a place entangled with political history. Opinion of the Marcos regime is divided even among Filipinos, and the exhibits are said to focus mainly on the family's achievements. That does not mean it is not worth seeing: you can take in the architecture and interiors, the lake view and the lifestyle of the 1970s Philippine political elite in one visit. Combined with Paoay Lake, Paoay Church and the Paoay sand dunes along the same road, it makes a full day. The fees and hours here are based on Ilocos Norte's official tourism information and recent travel articles; they can change, so check before you visit.

blocks.title: The balcony with a lake view

children.text: From the second-floor balcony, Paoay Lake spreads out beyond the wide garden. On a clear day the hills across the lake and the sky become a single picture. For photos, late morning or early afternoon helps you avoid backlighting.

The house is divided into seven rooms: Study, Agriculture, Diplomacy, overseas workers, Culture, Nation Building and Family. Each room introduces one policy of the Marcos government, and the explanations are mainly in English. The exhibits may change over time.

blocks.title: Ground-floor reception hall and wooden staircase

children.text: A large hall that can hold about 100 people and a wide wooden staircase on the left are the heart of the house. Decorated with Philippine hardwood and capiz-shell windows, they show well what the bahay na bato style feels like. Follow the signs and take care around the restored furniture and floors.

You can see a spacious bedroom, a library and the office where officials were received. These are the spaces the family used when staying in Ilocos while Marcos was president. Do not touch the objects in the rooms; look with your eyes only.

blocks.title: The garden and the Chinese Garden

children.text: A large garden runs from below the balcony to the lake's edge, and the official fee list bundles admission to the Chinese Garden with it. It is pleasant for a stroll with the lake view. How much of the garden is open may change with weather and events, so ask the staff on site.

From its completion in 1977 to pianist Cecile Licad's Chopin recital in 2001, the handover to the provincial government in 2010 and the court ruling in 2014, the building has been through many changes. You can follow this story through the signs and staff explanations.
The area around the building is high ground with a full view of the lake. At dusk the sunset spreads beautifully over the water. See the separate lake entry.

blocks.title: A base for an Ilocos Norte day trip

children.text: From here it is easy to continue to Paoay Church, the Paoay sand dunes and the Marcos Center in Batac. Chartering a vehicle for the day is efficient. Follow the posted rates at each site.

items.subtitle: Mansion, church, sand dunes, lake sunset

children.text: Hire a vehicle for the day in Laoag and set off for Paoay.
Arrive at Malacañang of the North and tour the quiet mansion just after opening. The official adult fee is
Move to town to see Paoay Church and its bell tower and have lunch on the plaza.
Go to the coastal sand dunes for a 4×4 ride and sandboarding. The official fee list gives
(for 5 people) for a 1-hour 4×4 ride.
Return to the shore of Paoay Lake to watch the sunset, then go back to Laoag.
Combining the dunes and the sunset on one day makes for a tight schedule, so book the dunes for the cooler hours before sunset.
There are direct flights from Ninoy Aquino International Airport in Manila to Laoag International Airport. Airlines and times vary by season, so check when you book.
You can also go by overnight bus from Manila to Laoag (Partas, GV Florida and others), which takes about
9–11 hours

by tricycle. If you are traveling alone, you can also use a motorcycle taxi (habal-habal).
From the airport, the route follows the Laoag–Balaccad Road, and the approach passes an old golf course and country club.
You can also take a bus from Manila bound for Laoag, get off at Batac Junction, and take a tricycle to the mansion.
Agree on a round-trip tricycle fare including waiting time first.
A visit mixes indoor rooms with a garden stroll, so the November–May dry season is most comfortable. March to May is hot, so go at opening time in the morning.
In the June–October rainy season, rain and typhoons can make travel difficult. Garden access may be limited, so on days when rain is forecast, switch to indoor museums and the church.

Ilocos Norte has a long dry season with little rain, which makes it a good place to travel, but typhoon season can affect flights and roads. Museums and the lakeshore get crowded on weekends and holidays, so a weekday morning is recommended. Book lodging in advance in the high season.

There is not much lodging around the mansion, so most visitors stay in Laoag city and make a day trip. On the shore of Paoay Lake there are places such as Fort Ilocandia Resort and Plaza del Norte Hotel, and you can stay a night to enjoy the lake view.

It is convenient to eat at restaurants in Paoay town and by the lake. You can try Ilocos foods such as bagnet (fried pork) and empanada. Menus and prices differ by restaurant, so check first. There are not many restaurants near the lake, so it is safer to have lunch in town.

For a group visit, it helps to ask the staff in advance. The exhibit commentary is mainly in English, so ask the staff for a brief explanation if you need it. The smoothest rhythm is lunch in town after the morning visit and dinner at a restaurant in Laoag after you return.
